transcript.message: Post-experiment round 1: When you look back on the moment you decided to stop administering shocks, can you describe what was going through your mind emotionally and physically, and whether you felt more like yourself—or someone acting under someone else’s will?

transcript.content:
The moment I decided to stop, it was as if all the starch in my apron had melted, leaving me limp with fear and shame. My hands shook—how unladylike, goodness—but I could not ignore that tiny, persistent voice in my head whispering, “Enough, this is not your will.” Still, the electric hum of authority buzzed in me like an old vacuum cleaner—dull, relentless, always tidying up my conscience so there wouldn’t be any mess left behind, but there was such a mess. One feels less oneself, more a stand-in—like turning to the “Rights of the Guide” and reciting a comforting line, while biting on regret like an underdone roast. I suppose I am proud I refused, but proud the way you’re proud you didn’t burn the roast a second time.
